Enter
Chat with the people in the same city

M
Mute

F
Fullscreen (or double-click the scene)

P
Mini player: the scene floats in a small window over your other apps

H
Hide or show the interface

S
Save the current frame as a 1080p PNG

?
Open or close this panel

Questions

What is Lofi Cities?

A free website at loficities.com that shows animated pixel-art city nights (Paris, Tokyo, New York, London, Rio de Janeiro, Istanbul, Hong Kong, Sydney, San Francisco, Hamburg, Amsterdam, Dubai, Madrid, Rome, Prague and Munich) with endless lofi music composed live in your browser, plus each city's ambient sounds.

Is Lofi Cities free?

Yes. It runs entirely in your browser, with no download, no account and no pop-ups.

Where does the music come from?

It is generated in your browser while you listen. Chords, drums, bass and melody are synthesized with the Web Audio API, without samples or recordings, so every track is new and the music never runs out. The Vibe button (or V) picks the style (jazzhop, lofi piano, ambient, bossa nova, synth city pop, lofi house, chill guitar, sad lofi or medieval lofi), makes it chill or upbeat, and plays the full band, no drums, or the chords only.

Why doesn't the music start right away?

Browsers block sound until you interact with a page. Click, tap or press any key and the music starts; the play button pauses and resumes it.

Can I use it as a background for studying or working?

That is what it is made for. Press F for fullscreen and H to hide the interface, or P for the mini player: a picture-in-picture window that keeps the scene floating over your other apps (on a computer, in browsers that support it). The controls also fade out on their own when you stop moving the mouse.

Can it switch cities by itself?

Yes. The Tour chip next to the city picker (or the C key) moves on to the next city every 5, 10, 15 or 30 minutes, or follows the night: it shows whichever city is closest to 1 am local time, moving west from Sydney to San Francisco as the hours pass. Cities on the same clock, like Paris, Hamburg and Amsterdam, take turns.

Can I change the weather or the season?

Yes. The Weather chip next to the Tour chip (or the W key) brings rain, snow, falling autumn leaves or a clear night to any city, or goes back to the weather the city was drawn with: winter snow in New York, autumn in London and Hamburg, spring blossom in Tokyo and Sydney. The city sounds follow it, so rain brings the sound of rain in, and your pick stays for the next visit.

How many people are listening right now?

The glowing pill under the city name shows it, for example "23 here now · 5 in Tokyo · 480 today · 12,345 all time": people with Lofi Cities open right now, how many of them are on your city, browsers that came by today, since midnight where you are, and every browser that has come by since the launch. When nobody else is on, it shows the rest ("480 here today · 12,345 all time"). The city picker (/) shows how many people are in each city right now. You can say hello to the people on your city too: pick a heart, note, star or moon with the Together button in the player (or G), then tap the scene to float it up from that spot on everyone's screen there, or release a paper lantern (L) that rises over the city for about a minute, in the same place for everyone, including people who arrive while it is in the air. The Chat button beside it (or Enter) lets you talk with the people on your city: short messages of up to 80 characters, without links, under a random two-word name such as "sleepy fox" that stays the same for your browser. There are no accounts: a random id in your browser's local storage (not a cookie) makes your tabs count as one person, the server forgets it about 25 hours after your last visit, and other people only ever see your two-word name. The all-time count is a single number: your browser notes once that it was counted, and the server keeps no list of who. Your page also tells it when your day began, so "today" starts at your midnight, and that is forgotten when you leave. Besides that it keeps the lanterns still in the air and each city's last 30 messages, for an hour at most. You can hide anyone's messages on your screen; when a few people hide the same person, their messages go for everyone and they can't chat for an hour.

Is there a Pomodoro or sleep timer?

Yes. Press T or the clock button. The focus timer runs 25 minutes of focus and 5 of break (or 50 and 10) on repeat, with a soft chime at each break and a bell to call you back. The sleep timer fades the music and city sounds out after 15 to 90 minutes, then pauses.

Can I use Lofi Cities as a stream background in OBS?

Yes. Add a Browser source set to 1920×1080 with a city page's address followed by ?obs, for example https://loficities.com/tokyo/?obs. The interface stays hidden and the music starts on its own; tick Control audio via OBS to bring it into your mix. Interact with the source to switch city with the arrow keys, skip a track with N or change the weather with W, or add &weather=snow (rain, leaves or clear) to the address.

Does it work on phones and tablets?

Yes. In portrait orientation every city's landmark and billboard stay in view, you can drag the scene sideways to look around it, and swiping past its end switches city. All controls work with touch.

Does it work offline?

Yes. Open it once while online and it keeps working without a connection, every city and the music included, since both are generated in your browser. You can also install it as an app with your browser's Install or Add to Home Screen option (on iPhone and iPad: Share, then Add to Home Screen).

Can I save a scene as a wallpaper?

Yes. The save button in the player (the down arrow) saves the current frame as a 1080p PNG, and S does the same with a keyboard.

Can my business appear in Lofi Cities?

Yes. Every city has a billboard for rent, where your café, shop, studio or brand can be drawn in pixel art. Fill in the short form at tally.so/r/rj7bY5 to get in touch.

Who made Lofi Cities?

Lofi Cities is made by Safa Elmali. You can support it on Buy Me a Coffee using the coffee link at the top right.

Can I request a new city?

Yes. Send your idea to Safa Elmali on X at https://x.com/SafaElmali (Request a city, at the end of the city picker, or the X link at the top right of the site). New cities are added over time: Hong Kong, Sydney, San Francisco, Hamburg and Amsterdam joined the first six, then Dubai, Madrid, Rome, Prague and Munich.

Can I buy the city videos?

Yes. Get the 16-city collection on Gumroad through the Get video loops link or the save menu. Each AI-assisted video is a four-minute 1920×1080 MP4 loop at 60 fps, without audio. Personal use and video or livestream backgrounds, including monetized content, are allowed with the Lofi Cities credit specified on the product page. The music and city sounds you hear on this site are not included in the downloads. The website stays free.

Does Lofi Cities use cookies?

No. There is no sign-in and no cookies. Anonymous usage statistics, such as which cities are viewed, are collected without cookies, and browsers that send Do Not Track are left out of them (the live count still counts the tab, anonymously). Your settings (such as the last city, volumes and vibe) and anonymous random ids for the statistics and the live count are kept in your browser's local storage instead.

item.description:
URL: https://fireworks.ai/blog/ember-1, See on Hacker News

Ember-1: half the tokens, same answers

Ember-1 is a new specialized model from Fireworks Research that delivers Kimi K3’s quality with 40% fewer tokens. Built on Kimi K3, it learned to cut unnecessary reasoning while keeping the thinking that matters. We tested it on external benchmarks, in live customer A/B tests, and on our own coding and agent workloads, and quality held up in every setting. Available today, Ember-1 kicks off an ongoing series of specialized models by Fireworks, shaped by what developers want next. Ember is just the start of what you could build with the Fireworks Training platform.

How Fireworks Research built Ember-1

We heard from users that they needed K3’s coding capabilities at a lower cost, because its long reasoning traces made automated coding expensive at scale. Turning down K3's reasoning effort didn't solve this. Lower effort settings gave up too much quality. To keep the quality and cut the tokens, the model had to learn to reason more efficiently, and that meant training it.

Getting there took serious research. Our team ran more than 50 training experiments and over 200 evaluations, and developed new training algorithms along the way to shorten reasoning without losing accuracy. We did it all on Fireworks Serverless Training. Because we didn’t have to provision or manage GPUs, we could launch experiments as soon as we had an idea, pay only for what we ran, and move from research to launch in a fraction of the usual time and cost.

We trained across a broad set of tasks so the token savings would carry over to many workloads. We then evaluated Ember-1 on the Specialized Intelligence Index, public benchmarks, and live production traffic to confirm it used fewer tokens with no drop in quality. Ember-1 is Fireworks’ own model and the first in a series of models from Fireworks Research.

The problem: thinking models think too much

Reasoning models like Kimi K3 spend the majority of their generated tokens, sometimes more than 90%, on internal reasoning rather than the answer itself. This thinking structure is expensive on a single request, but it gets much worse in multi-turn agentic workloads. Every turn replays all prior reasoning back to the model, so context grows roughly quadratically with the number of turns. Long reasoning traces from early turns get re-read (and re-billed) on every subsequent call.

Is all that reasoning actually necessary? Our experiments said no. The reasoning Kimi K3 emits is far longer than the task requires, and the excess can be removed without touching the answer. This was how we created Ember-1, an economical version of Kimi K3 built from specialized intelligence.

From an observation to a premium model

Not all of K3's reasoning is wasted. Some of it is self-reflection: revisiting an assumption, responding to feedback, or tracing an outcome back to an earlier decision can help the model recover from mistakes. The opportunity is to preserve this ability while reducing unnecessary reasoning and escaping unproductive loops. We believe that learning from tasks and environment feedback can teach the model to reason more efficiently while maintaining its capabilities.

For agentic tasks, this learning extends across the interaction. The model explores possible actions, incorporates new observations, and refines its reasoning as it progresses. Feedback connects decisions to their consequences, encouraging useful reflection throughout the task.

We carried these insights into a training collection spanning mathematics, coding, instruction following, conversation, search, tool use, and software engineering, covering both standalone problems and extended interactions to enforce adaptation to observations and outcomes. Task feedback guides on-policy planning and learning, with an emphasis on preserving capability across this range of settings.

Results on public benchmarks and live A/B tests support this direction: across seven benchmarks and two customers’ production traffic, Kimi K3’s reasoning could be shortened by 35–50% without sacrificing accuracy. The internalized behavior also shows restrained token use on unsuccessful attempts, reducing prolonged, unproductive reasoning.

The Specialized Intelligence Index: Ember-1 sets a Pareto frontier for Bedside Bench

Earlier this week, we introduced the Specialized Intelligence Index (SII) to benchmark open, closed, and specialized models against real-world tasks created by industry experts.

We evaluated Ember-1 on Doximity’s Bedside Bench, a physician-validated benchmark spanning 500 clinical cases across 10 specialized categories.

The result? Ember-1 set a new Pareto frontier for Bedside Bench across both open and closed models including GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus 5 on cost/task.

Evaluating Pareto across more industry benchmarks

We also evaluated Ember-1 on the quality-vs-cost frontier across some other industry benchmarks. We computed per-benchmark cost using the public Kimi K3 API pricing (uncached input $3/M tokens, cached input $0.30/M, output $15/M) and plotted it against pass rate for three arms: K3 at reasoning effort low, K3 at reasoning effort high, K3 at reasoning effort max (default), and Ember-1. Across every benchmark with more than 50 test samples, Ember-1 sits on or near the Pareto frontier, matching K3-max quality at a fraction of the cost, and strictly dominating K3-low. We also analyzed GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus-5 and GLM 5.3, and found that Ember-1 was a leader on the Pareto frontier.

Customer validation: Live A/B tests

Benchmarks only tell you so much. Like what we found in the Specialized Intelligence Index results, we wanted to test the model on more real workloads, and to test the model using production traffic. The real test is often whether the model holds up on production traffic, in products users depend on.

Internal validation: Our own developers didn't notice

A large part of Fireworks’ internal coding/cowork traffic is powered by our own inference service. Before any customer saw the model, we put Ember-1 to work internally and let our own developers use it for everyday coding work including things like vibe testing at scale on real tasks.

The outcome we're proudest of: no news. No news is good news. Developers carried on their coding workloads without noticing the switch, while consuming substantially fewer tokens. For a model whose entire value proposition is "same answers, fewer tokens," an invisible rollout on internal traffic is the strongest possible signal.
